lessons.title: AI Risks: Bias, Privacy, Security and Hallucination

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real or hypothetical AI use case you know something about (a chatbot, a scoring model, a recommendation engine). Write a half-page naming which of the four risk categories from the lesson -- bias, privacy, security, hallucination -- applies most directly to it, with one concrete sentence on what could actually go wrong if that risk went unmanaged.
slots.deliverable: A half-page written risk note for one real or hypothetical AI use case, naming its primary risk category and a concrete failure scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: For the use case you picked last hour, name who would hold each AI governance role from the lesson (model owner, ML engineer, risk/compliance reviewer) and which existing data governance body from earlier in this career path (a data owner, a steward, the governance council) that role would report into or coordinate with, instead of inventing a brand-new parallel structure.
slots.deliverable: A short written role map naming an AI governance role for your use case and the existing data governance structure it plugs into.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a training data governance checklist for your use case answering the lesson's core questions in writing: where the training data would come from, who would have to approve repurposing it for this model, and whether its original collection consent actually covers training a model on it.
slots.deliverable: A written training-data checklist answering the source, approval, and consent questions for your chosen use case.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the data quality dimensions from this career path's Data Quality Management course, write one SQL-style profiling check (or a described equivalent if you don't have a live dataset) you would run on your training data before training, then write a second check comparing the training population's distribution across one key segment (region, age band, customer type) against the population the model will actually be applied to, to spot a representativeness gap that could introduce bias.
slots.deliverable: One written data-quality check and one written representativeness/bias check against a training dataset, each with its intended result stated.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a labeling governance process for your use case's training data: who labels it, how label quality gets checked, and how disagreements between labelers get resolved. Then write one paragraph on whether synthetic data would be an appropriate substitute or supplement for any part of this dataset, and what governance question (realism, leakage of real individuals' patterns, disclosure to downstream users) you would have to answer before using it.
slots.deliverable: A written labeling governance process (labeler, QA step, disagreement resolution) plus a synthetic-data suitability note for your use case.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a six-field model card for your use case (intended use, out-of-scope use, training data summary, one evaluation metric, known limitations, owner and review date), then add two more entries to it: a model inventory record (model name, version, owner, status) in the format a registry would store, and a one-line lineage statement naming which source data and which pipeline step the model's training extract actually came from.
slots.deliverable: A complete model card for your use case plus a registry entry and a one-line AI lineage statement for the same model.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a versioning scheme for your model (what changes bump a major version versus a minor one -- retraining on new data, a feature change, a hyperparameter tweak) and then design the approval workflow it has to pass through before a new version reaches production: who reviews it, what the model card and quality/bias checks have to show, and who can reject it.
slots.deliverable: A written model versioning scheme plus a step-by-step approval workflow diagram or list for promoting a new model version to production.

slots.practicalActivity: Model governance lab: take the model card, inventory entry, lineage statement, versioning scheme, and approval workflow you've built across the last two slots and walk one hypothetical new model version through the entire approval workflow end to end, writing down what each reviewer would actually check at each step and where it would get blocked if the model card were missing a field.
slots.deliverable: A written end-to-end walkthrough of one model version passing through your full approval workflow, naming what each reviewer checks.

lessons.title: Prompt and Output Governance for Generative AI

slots.practicalActivity: Write an access control matrix for your model's full lifecycle (who can view training data, who can trigger retraining, who can approve a production deployment, who can query the live model), applying least-privilege from this career path's Data Security, Privacy and Classification course. If your use case is generative, add one more row: what prompt-injection or sensitive-output risk the model faces and one specific input or output filter you'd put in place.
slots.deliverable: A written access control matrix across your model's lifecycle, plus a prompt/output governance control for a generative use case.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a monitoring plan for your model naming at least two metrics you'd track in production (one performance metric, one data/prediction drift metric) with an explicit threshold for each that would trigger a review. Then write a short incident response runbook for the specific failure mode that worries you most about this model (a biased output, a security breach, a hallucinated answer sent to a customer): detect, contain, notify, remediate, in that order.
slots.deliverable: A written monitoring plan with two named metrics and thresholds, plus a four-step incident response runbook for one specific failure mode.

slots.practicalActivity: Security and monitoring lab: combine the access control matrix, the monitoring plan, and the incident response runbook into one operational security-and-monitoring section you could attach to your model card, and walk through one simulated incident (a drift alert firing) from detection through your runbook's steps to a stated resolution.
slots.deliverable: One combined security/monitoring section for your model card, plus a written walkthrough of one simulated drift incident resolved via your runbook.

slots.practicalActivity: Run your model through a five-point risk checklist (risk tier, data provenance, bias and fairness, model documentation, monitoring plan) and assign it an explicit risk tier -- low, moderate, or high -- with one sentence justifying the tier. Then name which named AI governance framework from the lesson's overview (such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework) that risk tier and its required controls map most closely onto.
slots.deliverable: A five-point risk checklist run against your model with an assigned risk tier, plus a named framework mapping for that tier.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one paragraph on which real regulatory regime from the lesson (such as the EU AI Act's risk-tier structure, or a sector-specific rule relevant to your use case) your model's risk tier would fall under and what obligation that would create. Then write a short audit checklist of five questions an internal AI auditor should be able to answer about your model using only the artifacts you've built in this course (model card, risk checklist, monitoring plan, access matrix).
slots.deliverable: A written regulatory-fit paragraph for your model's risk tier, plus a five-question internal audit checklist answerable from your own artifacts.

slots.practicalActivity: Responsible AI and risk practice: self-grade your own model against the five-question audit checklist you just wrote, honestly marking which questions your current artifacts actually answer and which ones expose a real gap (a missing owner, an unset monitoring threshold, an undocumented limitation) -- then write one sentence per gap on what you'd build next to close it.
slots.deliverable: A self-audit scorecard against your own five-question checklist, with a named fix for every gap found.

lessons.title: AI Governance Case Study: Credit Decisioning
AI Governance Case Study: Customer-Facing Generative AI

slots.practicalActivity: Following the structure of both case studies (risk tier, data provenance, bias/fairness, documentation, monitoring), write your own one-page walkthrough for a third scenario of your choosing -- a high-stakes decisioning model and a customer-facing generative one are both fair game -- naming the specific control each case study's model needed that a lower-risk model wouldn't.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written case-study walkthrough for a third AI scenario, naming the risk-specific controls it needs.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch the operating structure for an organization-wide AI governance program: which existing body (from this career path's program management content) would approve new models, what the intake process looks like for a new AI pilot before it gets built, and which of this course's artifacts (model card, risk checklist, monitoring plan) that intake process would require before any model reaches production.
slots.deliverable: A written AI governance program sketch naming the approving body, the intake process, and the required artifacts before production.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a one-page AI governance program proposal for a real or realistic organization of your choosing, including a risk-tiering checklist, a model card template with its six fields, a monitoring and incident-response plan, and the governance body that would own approving new models going forward.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written AI governance program proposal covering risk tiering, a model card template, monitoring/incident response, and program ownership.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can run a real AI or ML use case through a documented governance process end to end -- training data provenance and bias checks, a model card, a versioning and approval workflow, access controls, production monitoring with drift thresholds, an incident response runbook, and a risk tier mapped to a named regulatory framework -- the specialized AI governance layer this career path adds on top of its core data governance foundation.
